LOCAL PYTHON + PINNED NATIVE ENGINE

Run the local workbench.

The source is public on GitHub. Get the complete research-release package for source plus the optional prebuilt lab files. The package retains large research archives. The native solver is built locally. Physical force accuracy remains unqualified.

SolderShape runs locally. This website does not execute the solver or accept PCB uploads. You need Python 3.12 or newer, a C compiler, make and a modern browser. The application uses Python's standard library. The first setup downloads two hash-pinned upstream archives and builds Surface Evolver.

Start from the source directory

git clone https://github.com/steph4n-gh/soldershape.git
cd soldershape
python3 tools/setup_engine.py
python3 -m soldershape serve --port 8765

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/board. The setup reports ready and the application header identifies the native engine. On macOS, the source also contains a double-click launcher. Apple Silicon macOS with Python 3.14 and Apple clang 21 is the exercised platform. Other platforms remain unqualified.

Follow the Board design decision

  1. Choose Load U1 / J16 worked example. The actual lower copper is 400 µm in diameter. Other joints remain unsolved. The app saves one prior input snapshot for Restore my previous inputs.
  2. Confirm upper diameter 400 µm, held gap 300 µm, local +X offset 240 µm, reference volume 40 nL and candidate volume 56 nL.
  3. Confirm surface tension 0.48 N/m, density 9 g/cm³ and gravity enabled. All process inputs are hypothetical.
  4. Choose Compute selected comparison. At 300 µm, only 40 nL meets the numerical rule of lateral restoration without upward separation.
  5. Choose Try a 330 µm held gap. This changes only the gap and computes both volumes again. Both now meet the same rule.
  6. Inspect the current inputs, numerical status and physical limits. Save the review, editable case and board-bound evidence, then follow Prepare a test for this board question.

The 300 µm reference predicts X/Z forces of −184.526/−181.284 µN. Its candidate predicts −164.385/+13.386 µN. At 330 µm, the corresponding forces are −169.063/−227.390 µN and −170.455/−82.276 µN. Changing the gap removes the original upward-force reason to exclude 56 nL. Two sampled hypotheses do not establish manufacturing tolerance, a physical error bound or a production volume.

Read the origin label beside the meshes. The initial verified recording and a fresh native computation are distinct. Editing the selection or an assumption clears the current result and its export links. A freely supported package needs a weight-support objective instead of this held-gap fixture rule.

Prepare a matching physical test

The local handoff at /lab#board-question asks for independent hot wettable rims, upper-pad geometry, liquid volume, held gap, offset, alloy, temperature, density, surface tension and hot force versus displacement. The existing 200 µm force fixture needs adaptation and qualification for this 400 µm joint. The separate 220 versus 270 µm height coupon tests supported clearance against a 185 µm target. It does not validate these forces.

Replay both recorded hypotheses

Download the recorded walkthrough evidence and extract the outer package. Keep its notices. It contains the unchanged native archives for both gaps. From a source checkout with the pinned engine installed, run these commands after replacing the example package path.

python3 tools/verify_board.py /path/to/package/gap-300/board-comparison.zip --replay
python3 tools/verify_board.py /path/to/package/gap-330/board-comparison.zip --replay

Passing replay establishes numerical agreement within the declared checks. The outer package's manifest.json identifies both original archives and their exact hashes. Its README explains verification and replay. Inspect the 300 µm review and the 330 µm review. Read the physical and numerical limits before interpreting either result.
